title: Classes and instances
hook: A class is a reference-type blueprint. new allocates an object on the managed heap; the variable stores a reference, not the bytes of the object. That is the model behind every service you inject in a microservice host.

sections.heading: Blueprint versus object
sections.prose: Microsoft’s class documentation treats a class as the type definition and an object as a heap allocation configured from that definition. The default accessibility of a top-level class is internal; public is an explicit choice when another assembly must construct or mention the type. There are no free-floating functions at the language level: even top-level statements compile into a synthesized class with an entry point. Nested types live inside another type and are a way to keep helpers off the assembly’s public surface.

snippets.label: Two variables, one Customer instance
snippets.explanation: Assignment copies the reference. Both names observe the same mutation, which is why a lease object passed through a pipeline is shared identity, not a snapshot.

sections.heading: When a class is the right type
sections.prose: Use a class when the type has identity, mutable collaboration, or inheritance. An SQS consumer host, a Redis connection multiplexer wrapper, or an auth token validator is a class: callers need to share one instance and its lifetime. Prefer sealed unless you have a designed virtual surface (module 05). Static classes (later in this module) are for operations with no instance state. Records (module 05) are still classes when you write record without struct — they add value equality on top of reference-type allocation.

sections.heading: What this page does not cover
sections.prose: Finalizers look like ~TypeName() members. You almost never write them; native cleanup belongs on IDisposable with using (module 06), and the GC story is module 14. Methods that appear to hang off String or IEnumerable without living in those types are extension members — C# 14 expanded that syntax, and it is taught in module 10 so this module stays on types you declare.

interviewTakeaways: Class variables hold references; assignment does not clone the object.
Default type visibility is internal; members default to private.
Choose class for identity and lifetime; choose struct for small copied data (later topic).
commonPitfalls: Assuming var copy = original clones a class instance.
Leaving a public mutable class as an implicit DTO and then using it as a dictionary key.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS objects are also reference-like: const b = a copies the reference. There is no struct equivalent; primitives are copied. C# makes the split a type declaration.
TS class emits a constructor function. C# class emits CLR metadata and a heap object with a method table. private in C# is enforced at run time.
